tone_statements.citation: Boyd, Virginia L. 1997. A Phonology and Grammar of Mbodomo. MA thesis, University of Texas at Arlington (per Glottolog/WALS refdb 1235; no fulltext located).
tone_statements.quote: Mbódɔ́mɔ́ has both lexical tone and grammatical tone. Lexical tone is predominately a feature of nouns and modifiers. The tone is lexical because it is manifested contrastively in identical environments. Verbs, unlike nouns and modifiers, do not have tone as a contrastive feature. All verbs in isolation have the same tone pattern, high-low. In the clause, tone on the verbs is determined by various grammatical features such as the imperative aspect, and person marking on verbs in declarative clauses [...] There are two lexical tones in Mbódɔ́mɔ́, high and low. [...] A limited number of words may have contour tones. While most words with contour tones are borrowed, not all of them are
tone_statements.locator: p.41, §2.4 'Tone' and §2.4.1 'Lexical tone'; TBU statement §2.3.1 p.28 ('The vowel is the tone-bearing unit')
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 level (H, L) + marginal contour (rising, falling) on a few words; downdrift

Ch.2 Phonology (pp.9-60) covers consonants, vowels, syllable structure (2.3; 2.3.1 'The vowel is the tone-bearing unit', p.28) and 2.4 Tone (pp.41-49: two lexical tones H/L on nouns/modifiers; verbs lexically toneless with a fixed H-L melody in isolation; downdrift; grammatical tone: L-dissimilation, person marking by verb tone). Full-text search of the whole thesis: zero occurrences of 'stress'; 'accent' only in 'accentuates'; 'intonation' only re question intonation (p.166). No statement on word stress/accent.

sources.note: First-hand analysis: Mbodomo has both lexical and grammatical tone. Two lexical tones, H and L, contrastive on nouns and modifiers (minimal pairs nú 'mouth' vs nù 'ground', lémbé 'tongue' vs lèmbè 'sand'); TBU = the vowel (nasals do not bear tone); a limited number of words carry contour (rising/falling) tones, not all borrowed; downdrift of H after L in compounds and larger constructions. Verbs are lexically toneless: all verbs HL in isolation, their surface tone assigned by grammar (imperative LHL pattern, subject-agreement person marking, perfective L / imperfective H on the root per Boyd…

sources.note: Per Olson 2026 sec. 3: gives examples where rightward H-spread (which in Gbanu applies to /HL/ nouns before a following TBU) has been generalised in other Gbaya languages to all /HL/ nouns regardless of a following TBU (Mbodomo: *HL > HH sound change; Bhofi, SE Bhogoto: synchronic across-the-board rightward H-spread); title indicates H-spread and H-raising in Gbaya nominal tone.
